messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jamal, an 18-year-old African-American police officer, sought help after a series of distressing experiences that had been escalating for months. His story began in childhood when he witnessed domestic violence between his parents. The sight and sounds of their arguments and the physical assaults were imprinted vividly in his mind as snapshots—moments frozen in time that continued to replay whenever something triggered them. Since then, Jamal has become acutely aware of perceived threats around him, particularly in unfamiliar places where he cannot assess potential dangers easily. This avoidance stems from a deep-seated fear that bad things will happen again and that he can’t rely on himself to prevent it. Each time he feels uncomfortable or sees someone acting suspiciously, his body tenses as if reenacting the traumatic scene of witnessing violence. When Jamal remembers the event, he experiences overwhelming grief, feeling like he is right back in those moments. The bodily sensations are so vivid that he often finds himself reacting with a heightened sense of alertness, even when there’s no immediate danger present. This hyper-vigilance has led him to notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in every environment, further heightening his anxiety. The fear of losing control and going crazy since the event exacerbates Jamal's negative appraisals about himself and his ability to handle situations. He often feels helpless, believing that he can’t prevent bad things from happening again. These beliefs make him increasingly anxious and wary of anything that might trigger memories or heightened alertness. At work, Jamal’s hyper-vigilance has become a significant challenge. His occupation requires him to navigate various environments, but the fear of encountering unfamiliar dangers keeps him on edge. When he is touched unexpectedly while patrolling or responding to calls, his body responds as if it were back in that traumatic moment. The unusual silence during patrols makes him feel like something dangerous is about to happen, and this constant monitoring of potential threats has left him feeling exhausted. Jamal’s negative appraisals have reinforced his avoidance behaviors and increased his perception of threat. He often questions whether he can trust himself to handle situations appropriately, which further contributes to his anxiety. Each time he experiences a trigger or encounters something that reminds him of the violence, it reactivates those traumatic memories and feelings of grief. What Jamal most fears is losing control completely and feeling like he’s going crazy. His negative appraisals have made him doubt himself so much that he has isolated himself from social situations to avoid potential triggers. This isolation has led to conflicts with his colleagues at work, who don’t understand why he seems so on edge all the time. Jamal finally sought help after a particularly distressing incident where he overreacted in response to an unexpected touch while patrolling. He realized that these experiences were impacting his ability to do his job effectively and was afraid of losing his career as well as his sense of self-worth. Jamal hopes for support in managing his triggers, reducing the intensity of his memories, and gaining confidence in himself again so he can return to feeling like a capable and reliable police officer.
